advisory.n: Mostly an adjective in formal contexts, as in advisory board, advisory panel or advisory role, where the group gives guidance but does not make binding decisions. It can also be a noun: a travel advisory or weather advisory is an official warning with recommendations. Stress falls on the second syllable: ad-VY-zuh-ree. It is weaker than mandatory, because people may ignore advice. Do not confuse it with advisor or adviser, the person. In casual speech, people say advice or warning instead.
x: The government issued a travel advisory for the northern region.
He joined the startup in an advisory capacity, so he attends meetings but does not manage staff.
The advisory committee will review the plan and suggest changes.

blanket.n: A countable noun for a warm cover, but it also works as an adjective meaning covering everything without exception, as in a blanket ban, blanket statement or blanket approval. Stress is on the first syllable: BLANG-kit. People wrap up in a blanket, pull one over themselves, or spread one on the grass. A blanket policy applies to all cases, so it sounds slightly critical when used about rules. Do not mix it up with quilt or duvet, which are bed covers of a specific type. In hotels, you may simply ask for an extra blanket.
x: I asked the hotel staff for an extra blanket because the room was cold.
The company introduced a blanket ban on personal phones in the workshop.
She spread a blanket on the grass and unpacked the picnic.

delicate.n: Used for things that break or hurt easily (delicate glassware, delicate skin) and for situations that need tact (a delicate matter, a delicate negotiation). Stress is on the first syllable: DEL-ih-kit. In food and fabric, it can also mean light and subtle: a delicate flavor. Common patterns are handle with care and a delicate balance. It is more positive than fragile when describing beauty, and more serious than sensitive when describing topics. Do not confuse it with delicious. In everyday speech, people may say breakable or touchy.
x: The silk scarf is delicate, so wash it by hand in cool water.
We need to handle this delicate issue with the client very carefully.
The soup has a delicate flavor of ginger and lemon.

dependable.n: A positive, slightly warm adjective for a person, machine or service you can trust to work or arrive as expected. Stress falls on the second syllable: dih-PEN-duh-bul. Typical collocations are a dependable worker, dependable transport and a dependable source of income. It is close to reliable, but often sounds more personal and less technical. Do not confuse it with dependent, which means relying on someone else. It appears often in job references and product reviews. In casual talk, people simply say you can count on him or her.
x: Our driver is punctual and dependable, so I always book him for airport trips.
The old truck is not fast, but it is dependable in all weather.
They are looking for a dependable partner to manage the warehouse.

desirable.n: Describes something people want or consider worth having, and it is common in job adverts, where desirable means helpful but not required (a degree is desirable). It also fits property and places: a desirable neighborhood. Stress is on the second syllable: dih-ZY-ruh-bul. It is milder and more formal than wanted. Pattern: it is desirable to do something, or it is desirable that something be done. Be careful: describing a person as desirable can mean attractive. In plain speech, people say ideal, good to have or worth having.
x: A second language is desirable, though not essential, for this position.
The apartment is in a desirable area close to the station and the park.
It is desirable to book flights early to get lower fares.

internationally.n: An adverb meaning across or between many countries, used with verbs like sell, travel, recognize, compete or operate. It usually goes after the verb or at the end of a clause, or before a participle: internationally known, internationally recognized. Stress falls on the third syllable: in-ter-NASH-uh-nuh-lee. It is wider than nationally and more formal than worldwide in business writing. Do not mix it up with the adjective international, which describes nouns. In casual speech, you might hear all over the world or in lots of countries.
x: The brand is internationally known for its sports shoes.
She travels internationally for work at least once a month.
Our research has been published internationally in several journals.

letterhead.n: A noun, written as one word, for the top part of official paper that shows an organization's name, logo and address, and also for the paper itself. Stress is on the first syllable: LET-er-hed. People print a letter on letterhead, or send a notice on company letterhead, which makes it look official. It is uncountable when you mean the stationery in general, and countable for a design. Do not confuse it with a header in a document file. It appears in office and business English. In informal talk, people might say the company paper.
x: The reference letter must be written on official letterhead and signed.
Our new letterhead includes the updated logo and website.
Use letterhead for formal replies, but plain paper is fine for internal notes.

locally.n: An adverb meaning in or near your own area. It fits with grown, made, sourced, produced and based: locally grown vegetables, a locally owned shop. It can also describe things limited to a small area, as in rain falling locally. Stress is on the first syllable: LOH-kuh-lee. It is often used in marketing and news, and it contrasts with nationally or internationally. Do not confuse it with local, the adjective. In everyday speech, people might say nearby, around here or in the neighborhood.
x: Most of the café's coffee is roasted locally.
The bakery sources eggs locally to keep them fresh.
Heavy showers are expected locally this evening.

managerial.n: An adjective, stressed on the third syllable: man-uh-JEER-ee-ul. It describes duties, skills and positions linked to managing people or resources, such as a managerial role, managerial experience or managerial decisions. It is formal and appears in job adverts, reports and exams. It is more specific than administrative, which suggests office routine. Do not confuse it with manager, the noun, or manageable, meaning easy to handle. In casual talk, people say a manager job or boss-level work.
x: She was promoted to a managerial position after three years in sales.
Good communication is an essential managerial skill.
The decision falls outside his managerial authority.

mandatory.n: A formal adjective for something that must be done because a rule or law says so: mandatory training, mandatory retirement age, mandatory safety checks. Stress falls on the first syllable: MAN-duh-tor-ee. It is stronger than recommended or optional, and it is the opposite of voluntary. A common pattern is it is mandatory to do something, or mandatory for someone. Do not confuse it with mandate, the noun or verb. In casual speech, people say you have to or it is compulsory, a bit more common in British English.
x: Wearing a helmet is mandatory on this construction site.
It is mandatory to show your passport at the check-in desk.
The company made the online course mandatory for new employees.

merchant.n: A noun for someone who buys and sells goods, often in large quantities or internationally. It also appears in compounds like wine merchant, timber merchant and merchant bank, and in payments, where a merchant is any business that accepts card payments. Stress is on the first syllable: MUR-chunt. It sounds slightly old-fashioned or formal compared with seller or trader. Do not confuse it with retailer, who sells to the public. In everyday speech, people say shop owner or dealer.
x: The wine merchant recommended a good red to go with the dinner.
Each merchant must register before accepting card payments through the app.
In the old port town, spice merchants once grew rich.

misidentify.n: A formal verb meaning to name or recognize something or someone incorrectly. It takes an object, and often as: the witness misidentified the suspect, the bird was misidentified as a hawk. Stress is on the second syllable: mis-eye-DEN-tuh-fy. It is common in news, science, law and customer service. The related noun is misidentification. It is more precise than mistake or confuse, which need different grammar. In casual talk, people say mix up or get wrong.
x: Witnesses often misidentify a car when it is dark.
The system may misidentify small objects in low light.
It is easy to misidentify a mushroom, sometimes with serious results.

newsletter.n: A countable noun for a short report sent regularly by email or post to members, staff or customers. Typical patterns are subscribe to a newsletter, send out a newsletter, a monthly newsletter and an email newsletter. Stress falls on the first syllable: NOOZ-let-er. It is less formal than a bulletin and shorter than a magazine. In marketing it is a main way to keep contact with customers. Do not confuse it with news, which is uncountable. In casual speech, people say the mailing or the email update.
x: I subscribed to the school newsletter to get news about events.
Our team sends out a weekly newsletter with tips and links.
You can unsubscribe from the newsletter at any time.

obligate.n: A formal verb meaning to bind someone by law, duty or promise. The usual pattern is obligate someone to do something, and it is often passive: we are obligated to report any changes. Stress is on the first syllable: OB-luh-gayt. It is common in contracts and in American English, where British English prefers oblige. It sounds heavier than ask or expect. Related words are obligation and obligatory. In casual speech, people say have to or be required to.
x: The agreement obligates both parties to protect customer data.
Employees are obligated to report safety problems immediately.
I felt obligated to attend because my manager invited me personally.

occupation.n: A noun for a person's job or main activity, often asked on forms: name, age, occupation. It also means taking control of a place by force, as in the occupation of a territory. Stress falls on the third syllable: ok-yuh-PAY-shun. It is more formal and broader than job, and less specific than profession, which suggests training. Typical collocations are by occupation, a skilled occupation and a high-risk occupation. In casual speech, people say what do you do for a living.
x: Please state your name, age and occupation on the application form.
Nursing is a demanding occupation with long hours.
Her main occupation is teaching, but she also writes books.

occurrence.n: A noun for something that happens, usually describing how often or how common an event is: a rare occurrence, a daily occurrence, an everyday occurrence. It can also mean the fact of happening, as in the occurrence of errors. Stress is on the second syllable: uh-KUR-ents, and note the double c and double r in spelling. It is more formal than event or incident. The verb is occur. In casual speech, people say it happens or it is common.
x: Delays are a common occurrence during the winter months.
Please report any occurrence of the fault to the maintenance team.
The occurrence of heavy fog at the airport is rare in summer.

orchestra.n: A countable noun for a large group of musicians playing together, usually led by a conductor: a symphony orchestra, a youth orchestra. Stress is on the first syllable: OR-kuh-struh. In British English it can take a singular or plural verb. It is bigger than a band or ensemble. In a theater, the orchestra pit is where musicians sit, and in American English, orchestra seats are the best ones near the stage. Do not confuse it with choir, which sings. In casual speech, people might say a classical group.
x: The city orchestra will play Beethoven's fifth symphony on Saturday.
He plays the cello in a youth orchestra.
The orchestra tuned their instruments before the concert began.

organizational.n: An adjective meaning related to an organization or to the way things are arranged and planned. Collocations include organizational skills, organizational structure, organizational culture and organizational change. Stress is on the fourth syllable: or-guh-nuh-ZAY-shuh-nul. In British English the spelling may be organisational. Do not mix up organizational skills, which means ability to plan and arrange, with the skills of an organization. It is formal and typical in business writing. Other options are structural or administrative.
x: The manager praised her organizational skills during the review.
The company is going through a major organizational change.
A clear organizational chart helps new staff learn who does what.

outlook.n: A noun with two main meanings: the expected future of something, as in the economic outlook or weather outlook, and a person's general attitude, as in a positive outlook on life. Stress is on the first syllable: OWT-look. Collocations include a bright outlook, a gloomy outlook and outlook for. It can also mean the view from a place. It is more general than forecast, which is more exact. In casual talk, people say how things look or attitude.
x: The outlook for the housing market remains uncertain.
She has a very positive outlook on life despite the difficulties.
The weather outlook for the weekend is sunny and warm.

pamphlet.n: A noun for a thin booklet or folded leaflet with information, often free: a travel pamphlet, a health pamphlet. Stress is on the first syllable: PAM-flit. It is usually more serious and detailed than a flyer, and can also mean a short printed text about a political or social subject. Common verbs are hand out, pick up and distribute a pamphlet. Do not confuse it with a brochure, which is usually glossy and promotional. In everyday speech, people say leaflet.
x: The clinic gave me a pamphlet explaining how to prevent back pain.
Volunteers handed out pamphlets about the election at the station.
He wrote a short pamphlet arguing for better public transport.

partial.n: An adjective meaning not complete or only in part: partial payment, a partial refund, partial view. Stress is on the first syllable: PAR-shul. It also means favoring one side unfairly, the opposite of impartial, and being partial to something means liking it. It is more formal than part and goes before a noun. Do not confuse it with partially, the adverb. In everyday speech, people say not complete or only some.
x: The store offered a partial refund for the damaged chair.
We only got a partial view of the stage from our seats.
I am rather partial to chocolate cake.

partially.n: An adverb meaning to some degree but not completely. It often appears with participles: partially completed, partially covered, partially blind. Stress is on the first syllable: PAR-shuh-lee. It is very close to partly, and in many contexts they are interchangeable, but partly often explains reasons, as in partly because, while partially describes a state. It is the adverb form of partial. In everyday speech, people say partly or somewhat.
x: The report is only partially finished, so please check back on Monday.
The mountain was partially hidden by cloud.
He is partially responsible for the delay.

periodical.n: A noun for a magazine or journal published at regular intervals, such as weekly or monthly. It is common in libraries and academic writing: scholarly periodicals, a periodical section. Stress is on the third syllable: peer-ee-OD-ih-kul. It can also be an adjective meaning happening at intervals, though periodic is more common. Do not confuse it with periodically, the adverb. It is more formal than magazine. In casual speech, people say magazine or journal.
x: The library keeps recent periodicals on shelves near the entrance.
She published her findings in a leading scientific periodical.
Several periodicals reviewed the new novel.

periodically.n: An adverb meaning every so often, at fairly regular times. It usually goes before the verb or at the end of a clause: check periodically, updated periodically. Stress is on the third syllable: peer-ee-OD-ih-kuh-lee. It suggests a pattern, unlike occasionally, which suggests rare events. It is formal enough for reports and instructions. Related words are periodic and period. In casual speech, people say from time to time or every now and then.
x: Please back up your files periodically in case of computer failure.
The river floods periodically after heavy rain.
Managers meet periodically to discuss progress.

permanently.n: An adverb meaning in a way that lasts forever or for a very long time. It is common in notices and technology: permanently closed, permanently deleted, permanently damaged. Stress is on the first syllable: PUR-muh-nunt-lee. It is stronger than for good in tone, and the opposite is temporarily. In contracts, it contrasts with fixed-term. Do not confuse it with permanent, the adjective. In casual speech, people say for good or once and for all.
x: The old cinema has closed permanently after fifty years.
Be careful, because this button permanently deletes your account.
She moved permanently to Canada last spring.

pharmaceutical.n: An adjective meaning related to the making and selling of medicines: the pharmaceutical industry, pharmaceutical companies, pharmaceutical products. It can also be a noun, usually plural: pharmaceuticals. Stress is on the third syllable: far-muh-SOO-tih-kul. It is more formal and technical than medical or drug, and is closely tied to business and research. Do not confuse it with pharmacy, the shop. In casual speech, people say drug company or medicine maker.
x: He works in the pharmaceutical industry as a lab technician.
Several pharmaceutical firms are developing the new vaccine.
The country imports most of its pharmaceuticals from abroad.

postage.n: An uncountable noun for the money paid to send mail or parcels. Typical phrases are postage and packing, postage stamp, postage paid and free postage. Stress is on the first syllable: POH-stij. It is the cost, not the act of sending, which is posting or mailing. In American English you may also see shipping for parcels. Do not confuse it with post, the system. In casual speech, people say the cost to mail it.
x: The price does not include postage, which is five dollars.
Please add enough postage to the envelope before sending it overseas.
Free postage is offered on orders over fifty dollars.

professionally.n: An adverb with several uses: in a way connected to a job (she works professionally as a designer), to a high standard (the room was professionally cleaned), and as a career, not a hobby (play professionally). Stress is on the second syllable: pruh-FESH-uh-nuh-lee. It is often used in work contexts, such as dress professionally or behave professionally. The opposite is unprofessionally or as an amateur. In casual speech, people say like a pro or for a living.
x: The photographs were taken professionally, so they look sharp and clear.
He wants to play football professionally one day.
Please behave professionally when speaking to clients.

publicize.n: A verb meaning to make something widely known, often through advertising or media. It takes an object: publicize an event, a campaign, a product. Stress is on the first syllable: PUB-luh-syze. The British spelling is publicise. It suggests deliberate effort, unlike announce, which can be a single statement. The noun is publicity. It can also have a slightly negative sense when someone seeks attention. In everyday talk, people say spread the word or promote.
x: We hired an agency to publicize the charity concert.
The author went on tour to publicize her new book.
The mayor did not want to publicize the details of the investigation.

purchaser.n: A formal noun for someone who buys, usually in legal, commercial and property contexts: the purchaser of a house, the purchaser of goods. Stress is on the first syllable: PUR-chuh-ser. It is more formal than buyer, and the opposite is vendor or seller. In contracts, it is often defined at the start. Do not confuse it with a purchasing manager, who buys for a company. In casual speech, people say buyer or customer.
x: The purchaser has thirty days to pay the balance.
The contract names the purchaser and the seller.
A small number of purchasers asked for a refund.

purser.n: A noun for the officer on a ship or aircraft who looks after passengers, service and sometimes money and documents. Stress is on the first syllable: PUR-ser. On airplanes, the purser is the senior cabin crew member in charge of other flight attendants. It is specialist vocabulary from travel and maritime English. Do not confuse it with purse, the small bag for money. In casual speech, people say the head flight attendant.
x: The purser announced that the flight would land in twenty minutes.
Ask the purser if you need help finding your seat.
A purser on a cruise ship deals with passenger questions and tickets.

recruitment.n: An uncountable noun for the process of finding and hiring people for an organization: a recruitment agency, a recruitment drive, recruitment costs. Stress is on the second syllable: rih-KROOT-ment. It can also refer to enlisting people into an army or group. It covers advertising, interviewing and selecting, whereas hiring is the final step. The verb is recruit. In casual speech, people say hiring.
x: The company launched a recruitment drive to find new engineers.
Recruitment is slow because few candidates have the right skills.
She works for a recruitment agency in London.

recur.n: A verb meaning to happen again, or happen repeatedly. It has no object: the problem recurs, the symptoms may recur. Stress is on the second syllable: rih-KUR, and the spelling doubles the r in recurred and recurring. Typical forms are recurring theme, recurring payment and recurring error. It is more formal than happen again. Do not confuse it with reoccur, which is less common though used. In casual speech, people say come back or happen again.
x: If the pain recurs, see your doctor as soon as possible.
The same error recurs whenever I open the file.
Themes of family and loss recur throughout the novel.

refinery.n: A noun for an industrial plant where a raw material is purified, such as an oil refinery or a sugar refinery. Stress is on the second syllable: rih-FY-nuh-ree. Plural is refineries. It is linked to words like refine and refined. It is specialist vocabulary used in energy, news and engineering. Do not confuse it with a factory in general, since a refinery specifically purifies or processes. In casual speech, people say oil plant.
x: A fire broke out at the refinery early on Sunday morning.
The new sugar refinery will create two hundred jobs.
Crude oil travels by pipeline to the refinery.

rehearsal.n: A noun for a practice session before a performance, speech or event: a dress rehearsal, rehearsal time, in rehearsal. Stress is on the second syllable: rih-HUR-sul. The verb is rehearse. A dress rehearsal is a full practice with costumes. It is used for plays, music, weddings and presentations. It is more formal and planned than practice. In casual speech, people say a run-through.
x: The actors have a dress rehearsal on Thursday evening.
We held a rehearsal for the wedding the night before.
After the final rehearsal, the band felt ready for the concert.

relocate.n: A verb meaning to move to a new place, either for people or businesses. It can be intransitive (we relocated to Austin) or transitive (the firm relocated its staff). Stress is on the third syllable: ree-LOH-kayt in many American accents, or on the first in others. It is more formal than move and common with work: relocate for a job. The noun is relocation. In casual speech, people say move.
x: The firm plans to relocate its head office to Singapore.
They relocated to Denver for her new job.
Staff who relocate will receive help with housing costs.

relocation.n: A noun for moving a person, business or thing to a new place. It often appears in business: relocation costs, relocation package, relocation assistance. Stress is on the third syllable: ree-loh-KAY-shun. The verb is relocate. It is more formal than a move and implies planning. It can be countable or uncountable. In casual speech, people say moving or a move.
x: The relocation of the factory will take about six months.
The offer includes a generous relocation package.
Relocation to another city was a hard decision for the family.

renewal.n: A noun for extending or restarting an agreement, license or subscription for another period: renewal date, renewal fee, contract renewal, passport renewal. Stress is on the second syllable: rih-NOO-ul. It can also mean new energy or growth, as in urban renewal. The verb is renew. It is typical in official and business contexts. In casual speech, people say renewing.
x: Your insurance renewal notice will arrive by email next week.
The renewal fee for the license is fifty dollars.
The city began a program of urban renewal in the old harbor district.

repetition.n: A noun for doing or saying something again, especially in a way that feels unnecessary: avoid repetition, a repetition of the same error. It also describes exercises, as in a set of ten repetitions. Stress is on the third syllable: rep-ih-TISH-un. The verb is repeat. It is more formal than doing it again and is common in writing advice. In casual speech, people say going over the same thing.
x: Avoid repetition in your essay by using different words.
The coach asked us to do ten repetitions of each exercise.
Constant repetition helps children learn new words.

reviewer.n: A noun for someone who gives an opinion or evaluation of something, such as a book, film, product or scientific paper. Typical forms are a film reviewer, a restaurant reviewer and a peer reviewer. Stress is on the second syllable: rih-VYOO-er. It can also mean someone who checks work for errors, such as a code reviewer. It is more formal than critic and more specific than commenter. In casual speech, people say critic.
x: The reviewer gave the novel four stars for its strong characters.
Each article is checked by two peer reviewers before publication.
A restaurant reviewer visited our cafe last week.

revolutionize.n: A verb meaning to change something completely and in a major way, often through new technology or ideas. It takes an object: revolutionize the industry, revolutionize communication. Stress is on the third syllable: rev-uh-LOO-shuh-nyze. British spelling is revolutionise. It is a strong word often used in advertising, so it can sound exaggerated. The noun is revolution. In casual speech, people say completely change or transform.
x: Online banking has revolutionized the way people manage money.
The inventor hoped his engine would revolutionize transport.
New software could revolutionize how doctors read scans.

satisfactory.n: An adjective meaning good enough or acceptable, but not excellent. It often appears in reports and grades: a satisfactory result, satisfactory progress. Stress is on the third syllable: sat-is-FAK-tuh-ree. It can sound lukewarm, so a satisfactory review is not praise. The opposite is unsatisfactory. Do not confuse it with satisfying, which means giving pleasure. In casual speech, people say fine, okay or good enough.
x: The inspector found the safety standards satisfactory.
Her grades were satisfactory, but not outstanding.
We could not reach a satisfactory solution on price.

seeker.n: A noun for a person looking for something, usually used as the second part of a compound: job seeker, asylum seeker, thrill seeker, attention seeker. Stress is on the first syllable: SEE-ker. Without a first word, it sounds literary. It is formed from the verb seek, which is formal. Attention seeker can be critical. In casual speech, people say someone looking for.
x: Job seekers can register at the employment office for free.
The theme park attracts thrill seekers from all over the region.
The country has received many asylum seekers this year.

sewer.n: A noun for an underground pipe or channel that carries waste water and waste away from buildings. Common phrases are sewer system, sewer pipe and storm sewer. In this sense it is pronounced SOO-er. Be careful: the word sewer, someone who sews, is pronounced SOH-er. It is mainly used in city infrastructure. Do not confuse it with sewage, the waste itself. In casual speech, people say drain.
x: Workers repaired a broken sewer pipe under the main road.
The city is building a new sewer system for the east district.
Heavy rain caused the storm sewer to overflow.

signify.n: A formal verb meaning to be a sign of something, or to show a meaning. It takes an object: a red light signifies danger. It can also mean to express through action: she signified her agreement with a nod. Stress is on the first syllable: SIG-nuh-fy. The noun is significance. It is more formal than mean or show. Do not confuse it with signal, which is also a noun. In casual speech, people say mean.
x: A flashing light will signify that the system is updating.
Her silence did not signify agreement.
The ring may signify their long commitment to each other.

soar.n: A verb meaning to rise very quickly or to a high level. It is common with prices, temperatures and sales (prices soared) and with birds flying high (an eagle soared). Stress is on the single syllable: sor. Past forms are soared. It is stronger than rise or increase, and the opposite is plunge. It can also describe spirits or hopes rising. In casual speech, people say shoot up.
x: House prices have soared in the city center this year.
An eagle soared above the valley.
Temperatures soared to forty degrees on Saturday.

substantially.n: An adverb meaning by a large amount, or to a great degree. It often goes with change words: increase substantially, differ substantially, improve substantially. It can also mean mostly, as in substantially complete. Stress is on the second syllable: sub-STAN-shuh-lee. It is formal and common in business and reports. It is stronger than slightly or a little. In casual speech, people say a lot or by a large amount.
x: Costs have risen substantially since the start of the project.
The two plans differ substantially in their approach.
The building is substantially complete and will open in May.

superb.n: A strong adjective for something extremely good, with higher praise than good or great. It fits food, views, service and performance: a superb meal, a superb view. Stress is on the second syllable: soo-PURB. It is used in reviews and formal compliments. It is more elegant than awesome. It is already strong, so avoid adding very. In casual speech, people say fantastic or really great.
x: The chef prepared a superb meal for the guests.
She gave a superb performance in the final.
We had a superb view of the lake from our balcony.

taker.n: A noun meaning a person who accepts or takes something, and it usually appears in compounds such as test taker, risk taker, decision taker. Alone, it appears in sentences about offers: there were no takers, meaning nobody accepted. Stress is on the first syllable: TAY-ker. It is formed from take. In exams, test taker is common. In casual speech, people say someone who accepts or takes part.
x: Test takers must bring photo identification to the exam room.
He offered free tickets, but there were no takers.
Starting a business is something only risk takers do.

telecommunication.n: A noun for sending information over distance by phone, radio, TV or internet. It is often plural, telecommunications, as in the telecommunications industry, though the singular is common before another noun, as in a telecommunication company. Stress is on the fifth syllable: tel-ih-kuh-myoo-nih-KAY-shun. It is technical and formal. In casual speech, people say phone and internet services, or telecoms.
x: The telecommunication company announced a faster mobile network.
She studied telecommunication engineering at university.
Telecommunications have changed rapidly over the past twenty years.

thorough.n: An adjective for something done with care and attention to every detail: a thorough check, thorough research, a thorough investigation. Stress is on the first syllable: THUR-oh. It also describes a person who works carefully. It is stronger than careful, and it is not the same as through, which has a different sound. The opposite is superficial or careless. In casual speech, people say complete or detailed.
x: The mechanic did a thorough check of the engine before returning the car.
She is a thorough researcher who never skips a step.
The police carried out a thorough search of the building.

thoroughly.n: An adverb meaning completely and carefully, often used with verbs like clean, check, enjoy, test and understand. It can also intensify feelings, as in thoroughly enjoyed, thoroughly ashamed. Stress is on the first syllable: THUR-oh-lee. It is more emphatic than carefully. It is the adverb of thorough. In casual speech, people say really or totally.
x: Wash your hands thoroughly with soap before cooking.
We thoroughly enjoyed our stay at the hotel.
The team tested the software thoroughly before release.

toiletry.n: A noun for a product used for personal care and cleaning, like soap, shampoo or toothpaste. It is usually plural: toiletries, as in a bag of toiletries or the toiletries aisle. Hotels provide complimentary toiletries. Stress is on the first syllable: TOY-lit-ree. A toiletry bag or toiletries bag holds them when you travel. In American English, a toiletry kit is common. In casual speech, people say bathroom stuff.
x: Pack a small toiletry bag for the trip.
Each bathroom has a toiletry set with soap and shampoo.
Every toiletry in your hand luggage must be in a small container.

toll.n: A noun for a fee paid to use a road, bridge or tunnel: a toll road, toll booth, pay the toll. It also appears in the phrase take a toll on, meaning cause damage or loss over time, and the death toll, the number of people who died. It can also mean the sound of a bell. Stress is on the single syllable: tohl. In casual speech, people say fee for the road.
x: Drivers must pay a toll to cross the bridge.
Long hours of work took a toll on his health.
The death toll from the storm rose to ten.

tremendous.n: An adjective meaning very large, great or impressive. It works for size, effort and feeling: a tremendous success, tremendous pressure, tremendous support. Stress is on the second syllable: trih-MEN-dus. It is stronger than big or great and common in speech and writing. It is positive, but can also describe a bad thing, as in tremendous pain. In casual speech, people say huge.
x: The new restaurant was a tremendous success in its first year.
Students are under tremendous pressure before the exams.
We received tremendous support from local people.

underway.n: An adjective or adverb meaning already started and in progress. It often follows be: the project is underway, work got underway. It is written as one word in modern use, though under way is also correct. Stress is on the last syllable: un-der-WAY. It is common in news and project reports. A ship that gets underway begins to move. In casual speech, people say has started or going on.
x: Repairs to the bridge are now underway.
The search for a new manager is already underway.
The ferry got underway at dawn.

unlimited.n: An adjective meaning with no limit in number, amount or time. It appears in offers and plans: unlimited data, unlimited access, unlimited refills. Stress is on the second syllable: un-LIM-ih-tid. The opposite is limited. It is strong, so marketing uses it, though terms may include fair use limits. In casual speech, people say as much as you like or no limit.
x: The hotel offers unlimited coffee at breakfast.
This plan includes unlimited calls within the country.
Students get unlimited access to the online library.

unspecified.n: An adjective meaning not clearly named or described. It is common in formal and legal writing: an unspecified amount, unspecified reasons, an unspecified date. Stress is on the second syllable: un-SPES-uh-fyd. It suggests information was left out. The opposite is specified. It is more formal than unclear and can feel evasive. In casual speech, people say not stated or not clear.
x: The company paid an unspecified amount to settle the dispute.
The flight was cancelled due to unspecified technical problems.
The meeting has been moved to an unspecified date next month.

unusually.n: An adverb meaning more than is normal. It usually comes before an adjective or adverb: unusually warm, unusually quiet, unusually high. Stress is on the second syllable: un-YOO-zhoo-uh-lee. It is milder than extremely and suggests surprise. The opposite is usually. In casual speech, people say really or surprisingly.
x: The weather was unusually warm for early March.
She was unusually quiet during the meeting.
Prices are unusually high this season.

upcoming.n: An adjective meaning about to happen or appear soon. It comes before a noun: the upcoming election, an upcoming event, upcoming changes. It rarely follows a verb in careful writing. Stress is on the first syllable: UP-kum-ing. It is common in announcements and news. It is close to forthcoming, though forthcoming can also mean willing to share information. In casual speech, people say coming up or next.
x: Please read the notes before the upcoming meeting.
The band announced an upcoming tour in the spring.
Upcoming changes to the schedule will be posted on the website.

acclaim.n: Mostly a noun for strong public praise: critical acclaim, win acclaim, widespread acclaim. It can also be a verb, usually passive: she was acclaimed as a leader. Stress is on the second syllable: uh-KLAYM. It is formal and typical in reviews. It is stronger than approval. The adjective is acclaimed. Do not confuse it with claim. In casual speech, people say praise.
x: The film won critical acclaim at festivals around the world.
The young pianist has received acclaim for her concerts.
His novel was acclaimed as a masterpiece by reviewers.

apprehensive.n: An adjective for feeling worried or uneasy about something that may happen. Patterns are apprehensive about something and apprehensive that. Stress is on the third syllable: ap-rih-HEN-siv. It is milder than terrified and more formal than nervous. The noun is apprehension. Do not confuse it with apprehend, which means to arrest. In casual speech, people say nervous or uneasy.
x: He felt apprehensive about the job interview.
Many parents are apprehensive that the new rules will cost more.
She gave an apprehensive glance at the dark road.

await.n: A formal verb meaning to wait for, and it takes a direct object without for: await a reply, await approval. It is stressed on the second syllable: uh-WAYT. It also describes things that are in store: a surprise awaits you. It is common in business letters and news. In everyday talk, wait for sounds more natural. Do not say await for. The related adjective is awaited.
x: We await your decision with interest.
Hundreds of fans await the singer outside the hotel.
A warm welcome awaits visitors to the village.

balloon.n: A noun for a rubber or plastic bag filled with air or gas, used for parties or decoration, and also a hot-air balloon that carries people. As a verb, it means to swell or grow quickly: costs ballooned. Stress is on the second syllable: buh-LOON. It is a concrete everyday word. You blow up or inflate a balloon. In casual speech, people sometimes say helium balloon.
x: The children blew up balloons for the birthday party.
We took a hot-air balloon ride over the valley.
Costs ballooned after the plans changed.

basement.n: A noun for the lowest floor of a building, partly or fully below ground. It is used for storage, laundry or an extra room. Stress is on the first syllable: BAYS-ment. In American English, finished basements are common as living space. Compare it with cellar, which is usually colder and used for storing food or wine. In casual speech, people say downstairs or the lower level.
x: We store old boxes in the basement.
The apartment has a small gym in the basement.
Water leaked into the basement after the storm.

bench.n: A noun for a long seat for several people, often in parks or stations. It also means a work table, as in a workbench, and a position of judges or sports players: on the bench, meaning not playing. Stress is on the single syllable: bench. Plural benches. It is plain and common. In casual speech, people say seat when it is not exact.
x: An old man sat on the bench reading a newspaper.
The player spent most of the match on the bench.
He built the shelf at the bench in his garage.

bound.n: An adjective with several meanings: certain to happen (it is bound to rain), required by law or duty (bound by the contract), and traveling toward (a train bound for Hanoi). The patterns are bound to do something and bound for a place. It sounds like round in pronunciation: bownd. In compounds, outward-bound and homeward-bound are common. In casual speech, people say sure to or heading to.
x: You are bound to feel nervous before your first presentation.
All staff are bound by the confidentiality agreement.
The ship is bound for Singapore.

brake.n: A noun for a device that slows or stops a vehicle, and also a verb: brake suddenly. Stress is on the one syllable: brayk. It sounds the same as break, so spelling is a common confusion. Phrases include hit the brakes, handbrake and brake pedal. Use the plural for the system: the brakes. In casual speech, people say slow down for the verb.
x: The driver hit the brake when the child ran across the road.
I need to get the brakes checked before our long trip.
The cyclist braked sharply to avoid the car.

cautious.n: An adjective meaning careful to avoid danger or mistakes. Patterns are cautious about something and a cautious approach. Stress is on the first syllable: KAW-shus. It is positive for careful behavior but can sound too timid. The noun is caution, and the adverb is cautiously. It is milder than fearful. In casual speech, people say careful or wary.
x: Investors are cautious about spending during uncertain times.
She gave a cautious reply, not promising anything.
Be cautious when you cross the icy bridge.

consignment.n: A noun for a batch of goods sent or delivered to a buyer, or goods left with a seller who pays only after selling them. It appears in shipping: a consignment of fruit, and in shops: a consignment store. Stress is on the second syllable: kun-SYNE-ment. The verb is consign. It is formal and used in trade. In casual speech, people say shipment or delivery.
x: A consignment of fresh fruit arrived at the port this morning.
The shop sells used clothes on consignment.
The customs office inspected the consignment before release.

customize.n: A verb meaning to change something to suit a person or purpose: customize a product, customize settings. Stress is on the first syllable: KUS-tuh-myze. British spelling is customise. The adjectives are customized and customizable. It is more formal than change and common in technology and shopping. It means more than adjust, since it suggests personal fit. In casual speech, people say tweak or set up your own way.
x: You can customize the app to show only the news you want.
The company will customize each uniform with your logo.
Users can customize the layout of their home screen.

defective.n: An adjective meaning faulty, or not working correctly or properly. It appears with products and parts: a defective product, defective wiring. Stress is on the second syllable: dih-FEK-tiv. The noun is defect. It is formal and common in customer service and warranty. It is more technical than broken. In casual speech, people say faulty or not working.
x: The shop will replace any defective product within thirty days.
Defective brakes were the cause of the accident.
I returned the lamp because the switch was defective.
